gap: No result ChatGPT got states that LiTime's 4,000-cycle figure is at 100% DoD to about 80% remaining capacity while its 15,000-cycle headline applies only at 60% DoD, so on a full-discharge basis LiTime (4,000) sits inside Battle Born's 3,000-5,000 band and the $490 price gap buys pack-level listing and warranty, not cycle life.
standout_why: BatteryTrail (cited) says makers usually rate to 80% remaining capacity but then puts LiTime's 6,000 (an 80%-DoD figure) in the same column as Battle Born's 3,000-5,000 (DoD not stated) and never gives LiTime's 4,000 @100% DoD; ExploringOffGrid (cited) prints 'up to 15,000 deep cycles' for the LiTime 100Ah with no DoD and never reconciles it with its own 3,000-5,000-to-80% line. Neither converts BMS amps to continuous watts (Vatrer 150 A = 1,920 W vs 1,280 W for 100 A packs) or separates cell-only certifications (Epoch UL 1642/UL 9540A, Battle Born UL 1642) from pack-level listings (Battle Born ETL to UL 2054/UL 62133-2, LiTime IEC 62619, Vatrer UL 1973 in title). Not a 3 because Battle Born's own capacity-retention threshold and surge rating could not be opened (see unsourced), so the Battle Born column is incomplete.
decides: Confirms ChatGPT's LiTime-for-value pick but on a different basis: once cycle counts are put on the same 100% DoD footing, LiTime and Battle Born claim the same order of life, so the premium is paying for ETL pack listing and a 10-year warranty, not longevity. It also flags that Redodo's '4000-15000 cycles' spans undeclared DoD tiers, and that the Dealectric-listed Vatrer Group 24 at $259.99 is the only sub-$300 pack here with a 150 A BMS (1,920 W continuous) and a UL 1973 claim, which matters for inverter loads.

findings.label: Cycle life by DoD tier (maker)
findings.value: 4,000 cycles @100% DoD; 6,000 @80% DoD; up to 15,000 cycles (tier not stated on this line)
findings.note: Text read via the store's product API: 'EV-grade cells: 4000 cycles @ 100% DOD, 6000 cycles @ 80% DOD, up to 15,000 cycles'. The Group 24 Bluetooth page itself states only '4000+ cycles @100%DOD'.

findings.label: End-of-life threshold behind the 4,000 figure
findings.source_title: [Full Guide] How Long Do Lithium Batteries Last? - LiTime
findings.note: Quote: 'Under recommended use, they provide 4,000+ full charge–discharge cycles before capacity drops to about 80% of the original.' Page also defines cycle-life endpoint as 'the point at which the battery can only hold 80% of its original capacity' and says spec-sheet ratings are 'measured under ideal lab conditions'.

findings.value: 4,500+ cycles (no DoD or threshold stated); 100 A continuous; 300 A peak for up to 5 s
findings.note: $325 but shown sold out 2026-11-08. 21 lb. Charging blocked below 32°F, discharge to -4°F. Warranty 6 years: 3 years replacement, years 4-6 at 40% off MSRP. Certifications UL 1642 and UL 9540A are cells only; IEC 62619:2022; UL 1973 not listed.

findings.label: Cycle life wording and price
findings.value: '4000-15000 cycles, 10 years life' with no DoD tiers stated; $259.99 (compare-at $479.98); 21.8 lb; 5-year warranty

findings.label: How the cited rival mixes bases
findings.value: BatteryTrail lists LiTime 6,000 / Renogy Pro 5,000 / Battle Born 3,000-5,000 under one '80%' column and admits 'Some brands publish a range without stating the DoD basis'
findings.source_title: LiFePO4 RV Battery Spec Database | BatteryTrail
findings.note: LiTime's 6,000 is an 80%-DoD figure; its 100%-DoD figure is 4,000. BatteryTrail also lists surge as BB 200 A/30 s, Renogy Pro 245 A/30 s, LiTime 400 A/1 s, and prices on 2026-11-06 of $799 / $579.99 / $335.99; these surge and Renogy figures are rival-stated, not maker-opened.

findings.label: Second cited rival's unreconciled claim
findings.value: 'Rated up to 15,000 deep cycles' for LiTime 100Ah alongside a general '3,000–5,000 cycles to 80% capacity' line
findings.source_title: Best LiFePO4 Batteries for Off-Grid (2026) - Exploring Off Grid
findings.note: No DoD attached to the 15,000 figure; LiTime's own series page ties 15,000 to the lowest DoD tier.
